items.title: Garena Showcases Palworld Online Mobile Gameplay and Opens Limited Pre-registration
items.summary: Pre-registration is currently only available in South Korea, but a new trailer offers a glimpse into the mobile version of the game.
items.content:
0 Источник: Garena / Pocketpair 1 September 2026, 13:39 Viktor Zaycev Pre-registration is currently only available in South Korea, but a new trailer offers a glimpse into the mobile version of the game.

Garena has unveiled a gameplay trailer for Palworld Online and opened pre-registration on Google Play and the App Store. For now, only users in South Korea can register, but the video provides a detailed look at the mobile interface and the adaptation of familiar mechanics.

The trailer showcased open-world exploration, battles, resource gathering, base building, and pal capturing. The core mechanics are implemented quite similarly to the original game. Additionally, cooperative raids, dungeons, PvP duels, and other multiplayer activities are announced.

The release of Palworld Online on Android and iOS is scheduled for 2026. Garena has not yet announced an exact date, although the App Store lists November 30. It is also unknown whether the launch will be simultaneous worldwide or if users outside South Korea will have to wait – the limited pre-registration suggests the latter.

Recall that Palworld Online will not be the only mobile spin-off of the franchise. A separate Palworld adaptation is also being developed by Krafton and PUBG Studios, but it does not yet have a release date.

items.title: Steam’s PvE Survival Crafting Fest offers up to 90% off on survival hits
items.summary: Valve continues to keep Steam's calendar packed with themed sales, and its latest event is aimed squarely at fans of one of PC gaming's biggest genres.
items.content:
Valve has been frequently release many varied official sales and events, cementing Steam's reputation for constant value through frequent discounts and widespread game participation. With the latest themed festival now live, it's the perfect week to pick up those survival or crafting games you've been eyeing.

The Steam PvE Survival Crafting Fest 2026 is now live, bringing discounts and demos for a wide range of games centered around exploration, crafting, building, and surviving against environmental threats and hostile creatures. The genre has become a major force on Steam, with hits such as Palworld and Enshrouded helping cement its popularity.

As usual, Valve has also released a tongue-in-cheek trailer hosted by Kaci Aitchison, giving players a quick tour of the event and highlighting some of the discounted titles. There are plenty of familiar names alongside lesser-known games, while numerous demos offer an easy way to try something before spending any money.

One particularly timely pick is Project Zomboid , which recently received its stable 42.20.0 update. The major update brings substantial changes to the game, including an overhauled map, expanded crafting systems, and multiplayer improvements, making the ongoing sale a good opportunity to jump into the zombie survival sandbox.

Meanwhile, Astroneer takes the survival-crafting formula into space. Players can explore colorful alien planets, reshape terrain, construct modular bases, travel between worlds, and gradually automate their operations as their interplanetary adventure expands.

Craftopia is another unusual option. Developed by Pocketpair, the studio behind Palworld , it combines farming, automation, dungeon crawling, hack-and-slash combat, and extensive base building. It's difficult to put into a single genre, but that's part of its appeal. For something more relaxing, Len's Island mixes farming, construction, exploration, and combat. You can grow crops and build a comfortable home before venturing into dangerous dungeons in search of valuable loot and completing quests scattered around the mysterious island.

These are just a handful of the games featured in the event, with plenty more discounts and demos available throughout the week. The Steam PvE Survival Crafting Fest 2026 began on August 31 and will run through September 7, 2026, giving survival fans one week to explore the deals.

As always, if you’re looking to get the most value from your gaming budget, be sure to browse our dedicated deals hub for the latest offers.

items.content:

(Image credit: Pocketpair) {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 34 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Growing infatuation with Steam player numbers as a means to gauge a game's success or popularity has ultimately misled a lot of people, worries Palworld liaison and Pocketpair publishing lead John Buckley.

Because Steam is both the dominant platform for PC gaming and the only major platform that shares live, granular player data, Steam player counts, particularly concurrent users, are regularly used as a measuring stick, or just as often, a bludgeon. It could be Arc Raiders, Palworld, Peak, How to Fish , or Baldur's Gate 3; gamers will put you under the SteamDB or Steam Charts microscope.

Buckley's regularly pushed back on the "dead game" doomsaying chucked at Palworld and countless other games over the years, arguing that player falloff is normal and expected, and that numbers often described as dire are in fact quite healthy. In an interview at Gamescom 2026 , he describes the Steam number chatter as part of a larger misunderstanding.

"The numbers are so distorted with Palworld," he says. "I so vividly remember the 2.1 million concurrent to half a million concurrent [period]. Some of the most viral posts at that time were, 'This is the biggest game dropoff of all time.' And I was like, half a million people playing a game at any one moment, it makes me want to be sick, how staggering that is."

Though Palworld was biggest on PC, it wasn't only on PC, and this is one problem with Steam math. We can estimate trends based on a game's Steam community, and Steam player numbers do have genuine value and applications, but we can't get a reliable picture of a multiplatform release. The factors driving spikes and dips in those numbers are also much more varied than whether a game is good or bad. Sales, update cadence, server downtime, time zones, and replayability can have a big impact.

Arc Raiders and Marathon aren't "dead" because their concurrent players dropped, Palworld lead says Palworld lead shrugs off "dead game" suggestions as its Steam concurrent player count is still huge Palworld has been "life-changing," lead says as it hits almost 1 million concurrent players on Steam

In a similar vein, Buckley looks at what concurrent Steam users can and can't tell us.

"And not to dog on SteamDB, because I love those guys, but I think of how public these numbers have become in recent years," he says. "People really love pulling these numbers up recently. Now we know why consoles don't like to share them."

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

As it happens, Sony recently began testing a tiny PS5 widget which , in some way, offers a snapshot of game activity not too far removed from Steam Charts. And even that small glimpse into the console black box seems to come with huge obfuscation.

"People look at these, and I think that's all really misunderstood now," Buckley continues. "I think people think 500,000 CCU one hour and 400,000 CCU one hour means 100,000 people stopped playing. That's not what it means, because any second two could log on and two could log off.

"I think we need to start sharing DAU [daily active users]. I wouldn't be against making DAUs public – the amount of actual people who played a game in one day. Because I think a lot of people would be shocked how different these numbers are. You know, a game that has 1,000 CCU could have 20,000 DAU. The numbers are quite different."

items.title: Palworld Meets Stardew Valley in Spirit Rancher
items.summary: Palworld Meets Stardew Valley in Spirit Rancher, A Cozy Creature-Collecting Farming Sim Where Crops Are Alive Catch spirits, battle and explore alongside them, borrow their power
items.content:
Palworld Meets Stardew Valley in Spirit Rancher, A Cozy Creature-Collecting Farming Sim Where Crops Are Alive Catch spirits, battle and explore alongside them, borrow their powers, and build an ever-growing farm fueled by the resources they produce.

"); //]]>--> MANILA, Philippines – August 27, 2026 – What if the creatures you collected in Palworld are also the crops and livestock powering your Stardew Valley-style farm? Independent Philippine game studio Yangyang Mobile is excited to announce Spirit Rancher, a cozy creature-collecting farming simulator where magical spirits aren't just companions, they're the foundation of everything you build.

In Spirit Rancher, players venture to discover and catch a variety of spirits, each with their own unique abilities and resources they can produce. Fight and explore alongside them, use their powers, then bring them home and design a ranch that would keep them happy and productive.

The happier your spirits are, the more your ranch can grow.

Instead of taking care of endless rows of traditional crops, players can build automated systems to move their resources around the ranch and experiment with different spirit combinations to create miniature ecosystems: one creature's produce becomes another's food, turning the right habitat into a self-sustaining production chain. The more efficiently your ranch runs, the more you can build, automate, and expand.

The result is a gameplay loop that combines the thrill of creature collecting with the cozy satisfaction of building, optimizing, and expanding a home of your own.

Catch and Collect Spirits: Explore the world, discover new creatures, and bring them home to become part of your growing ranch.

Fight Alongside Your Companions: Your spirits aren't just ranch residents. Take them with you and battle together on adventures.

Use Their Powers: Fuse with your spirits and harness their unique abilities yourself, using their powers to fight, explore, gather resources, and interact with the world.

Build Them a Home: Create and expand a ranch where your spirits can thrive. Build habitats and facilities around the creatures you've collected and the resources they produce.

Design a Growing, Living Ranch: Start small and gradually build a bustling home filled with spirits, facilities, resources, and interconnected production systems.

Explore a Story-Rich World: Meet a colorful cast of characters, form relationships, make choices, and uncover the mysteries surrounding the world of Spirit Rancher and the spirits that inhabit it.

Spirit Rancher is currently in development. It will be released in Steam Early Access in 2028.

items.title: Pokemon-channeling Palworld courts fans through addictive play
items.summary: It would be fair to say that I’ve been out of the loop on AAA games the last few years. Big studios pushing wildly expensive product on a mostly cynical
items.content:
It would be fair to say that I’ve been out of the loop on AAA games the last few years. Big studios pushing wildly expensive product on a mostly cynical audience growing more cynical by the day did not exactly inspire confidence.

Especially when a single game costs somewhere in the ballpark of $70 (and developers think that’s too low — see speculation of GTA VI’s eventual price tag later this year). The last time I paid full price for a game was the Resident Evil 4 Remake, which took me back to pre-ordering the original for the Gamecube back in 2005.

Pokemon fans have long known that the price of a game does NOT go down over time. Nintendo fans in general accept this as something of an axiom. I played the original generation in 1998 quite a bit. Heck, I got an emulator, ROM and printed guide/walkthrough so that I could play and beat the second generation in Japanese before it came to North America.

Suffice it to say, I was a big Pokemon fan. I was out until, to quote Michael Corleone, they “pulled me back in” through a friend. That would’ve been the sixth generation around 2014 or so. I got a 3DS, Pokemon X and found myself reliving part of my childhood. I enjoyed the seventh generation, even if they occasionally seemed to run out of ideas, such as the introduction of a sandcastle Pokemon (they had earlier made an ice cream Pokemon, as well).

Then they moved from the 3DS to the Switch, which I don’t have. Pokemon had always been a handheld game, so the move seemed like an odd decision. That being said, The Pokemon Company empire knows what it is doing. Other AAA games take somewhere around $200 million or more to develop and can easily flop or merely break even. A Pokemon game costs around $10 to $20 million to develop and can generate around $1.5 billion in direct game sales.

It seemed they were indestructible, untouchable and what’s more is they knew it. Forget quality, just slap the name Pokemon on the product and it would sell like hotcakes. What could possibly go wrong?

Enter Palworld, “Pokemon with guns,” made by rival Japanese indie company Pocketpair as an open-world adventure game populated by “Pals,” which the player can battle or capture for combat, base building or traversal.

The early access version was released in January 2024 and reached a total number of players exceeding 25 million within one month. It peaked at more than 2 million concurrent players shortly after launch, something most AAA games never achieve.

Since the 1.0 full release July 10, it has roughly 400,000 concurrent players at any given moment on Steam. Critics (and Pokemon fans) point to the drop from the peak numbers, but those numbers for a game that released more than two years prior is nearly unheard of.

It’s also currently on Steam for $30, which for something of this magnitude and scope is quite the deal.

Jumping in, I initially had a feeling that Palworld’s core gameplay mechanics were similar to Minecraft, though I wouldn’t really know firsthand. You punch the tree to get wood, you punch the rock to get stone, then make a woodcutting axe and pickaxe with the materials you just gathered, improving your capabilities, build a home base and expand from there, rinse and repeat.

The slow grind and requirement that you (or your industrious Pals) craft everything yourself really gives weight to everything. You didn’t just find those cold-resistant clothes in a chest, you had to make them yourself. You can build a ranch, capture some of the sheep-like Pals and they will drop wool. Or you can go fight wild ones, who drop wool and lamb chops for cooking later.

I can’t be the only one who always thought about eating some of the cute little monsters in Pokemon. After all, who wouldn’t want to try some Magikarp sushi? In Palworld, your monster buddies need to eat, too. Morality aside, you can feed bacon to the pigs, if you get my drift.

To repeat myself, I do not own a Nintendo Switch or its aptly-named successor, The Switch 2, so I have not been able to play the newer Zelda games, but the climbing, hang gliding and stamina management seem copied directly, from what I know. You would think Nintendo would get litigious, which brings me to the next point.

The Sunlit Isle (405, -483) Pros: Several crude oil nodes, easy to defend during raids Cons: No nearby ore Closest teleport: Sunlit Isle It's not the best spot for ore or stone, but the Sunlit Isle just east of Palworld's starting area makes early game crude oil farming a breeze with six nodes scattered across the land. It's not difficult to defend, and the pals living here are under level 10. I like building at the highest point along the island's south side, but there's a cute spot northeast with stone steps leading up to it that works just as well. Even if you intend to go elsewhere for ore farming, this is a great place to build a second base for a steady crude oil supply.

items.title: v1.0.3: Balance Adjustments & Bug Fixes
items.summary: \ Palworld version v1.0.3 has been released! ＝＝＝ \ ▼Items and Equipment ・Changed the unlock level of some Jetragon-related technologies from 79 to 70, and reduced the materials required for the Pal Gear used to ride Jetragon. ・Changed the t
items.content:
\

Palworld version v1.0.3 has been released!

＝＝＝

\

▼Items and Equipment ・Changed the unlock level of some Jetragon-related technologies from 79 to 70, and reduced the materials required for the Pal Gear used to ride Jetragon.

・Changed the technology unlock level of the Aquatic Construction Kit from Level 66 to Level 23, changed its Ancient Technology Point requirement from 4 to 1, and adjusted the required materials and work amount.

・Extended the duration of World Tree Holy Water.

・Reduced the weight of World Tree Holy Water from 1 to 0.1.

・Added World Tree Holy Water to the rewards for World Tree expeditions, World Tree fishing, and the Large Fishing Pond.

・Increased the amount of World Tree Holy Water obtained from Pals in The World Tree area.

・Increased the amount of World Tree Holy Water obtained from Teafant Spring.

・Adjusted the work amount required to craft the Ancient Armor series.

・Doubled the amount of Fiber obtained from trees.

▼Bases and Missions

・Reduced the building costs of the Crude Oil Extractor, High-Pressure Crude Oil Extractor, and Large Power Generator.

・Increased the crude oil production speed of the Crude Oil Extractor and High-Pressure Crude Oil Extractor.

・The base mission that requires building a Crude Oil Extractor can now also be progressed by building a High-Pressure Crude Oil Extractor.

▼Server Settings

・Added a server setting (bAllowEnemyCampSpawnNearBaseCamp) that disables the suppression of enemy camp spawns near player base camps.

\

▼Graphics and Display

・Adjusted the boundary display in some areas to make it easier to see from a distance.

・Improved the display quality of some objects in dungeons.

▼Sound

・Added a sound effect when using World Tree Holy Water.

\

▼Crashes and Progression Blockers

・Fixed an issue where the mission could become impossible to progress if the barrier was removed before accepting the main mission in Sunreach.

▼Multiplayer and Co-op

・Fixed an issue in co-op where lighting on the client side could display incorrectly after cutscenes or the ending played.

・Fixed an issue in co-op where some scenes could stutter during the cutscene that plays when entering The World Tree.

・Fixed an issue on dedicated servers where Fast Travel could activate unintentionally during Tower Boss battles.

・Fixed an issue on dedicated servers where Pals could appear to vibrate rapidly on the client screen.

▼Pals and NPCs

・Fixed an issue where the summoned Pal could stop fighting.

items.title: This New Survival Game Finally Clicked with Me, and I'm Never Looking Back
items.summary: Palworld 1.0 does a great job of easing you into its many complex systems.
items.content:
Survival games have been wildly popular for years now. I’ve dabbled here and there to see what the fuss is about, but I’ve always fallen off after a few hours. Usually, I get tangled up in one meagerly explained system after another until I lose track of what I’m supposed to do, and my time with the game peters out.

When Palworld 1.0 came out to rave reviews , I figured I’d give the genre another shot – and I’m glad I did. Palworld’s gradual, newbie-friendly onboarding helped me see what a whole lot of people have loved about survival games all along. Palworld made me a believer.

I’m glad I came in at the 1.0 mark, because I’ve heard Palworld had a much steeper learning curve out of the gate. But now, new players start with a series of missions designed to guide you through the game’s numerous systems . You learn how to punch trees to get wood to create a crafting bench. You learn how to make a club you can use to beat some Pals to death (it’s a dog-eat-dog world out there) to get wool. You then use that wool to make clothes. You set up a camp. You build a house. You activate a teleporter and explore deeper into the game world.

Before long, you’re gliding off cliffs Zelda-style before whomping on every Pal you see to catch them in spheres to put them to work. You can deploy them at your camp, ride them , or have them fight by your side to take on big roaming Pals and towering bosses . It’s a blast. And there’s no way I would have stuck with it if it hadn’t held my hand and eased me into the systems that make up the game.

I still have a long way to go, because I was nowhere near powerful enough to defeat the first boss solo. But those early missions gave me a much-needed handle on what else I can spend my time doing as I level up enough to become a threat. There's a vast world out there I can keep exploring, all while catching Pals and building up my base. I’m having a blast doing it.

Palworld’s 1.0 is available on Steam , Xbox , and PS5 . It costs $29.99, but you can save a few bucks on a Steam copy at Fanatical , which is currently running its summer sale .

Chris Reed is a commerce editor and deals expert for IGN. He also runs IGN's board game and LEGO coverage. You can follow him on Bluesky .

items.title: Palworld 1.0 Review – Bigger, Better, and Still Brutally Addictive
items.summary: Palworld 1.0 is crammed with new content. More Pals, better quests, and a fully realized world for new and returning players to explore.
items.content:
Remember Palworld ? Well, the controversial game from Pocketpair finally has a 1.0 release. After two years, this feels like a very different animal than the one I initially encountered. The quest system is more complete, the UI is polished, and the world feels much more interconnected than before. While there are still some rough edges, this version of Palworld is a vastly improved one.

Now, I haven’t been keeping up with every iteration of Palworld released up to this point. So I’m not clear on how gradual or sudden these changes might be. But oh man, the quest system feels like night and day. You’re fed a steady stream of quests from the jump. They pair nicely with the tech tree, they appear on your map, and they sync with your compass. Yes, this is incredibly basic stuff. We figured out quest design decades ago. But you really appreciate the elegance of that design when it’s missing. Then when it finally shows up? It’s water in the desert.

Beyond the quests, it turns out Palworld works much better with connective tissue in place. Fast travel points, side quests, a detailed map, and distant objectives (like a floating island on the horizon) all make the world feel more tangible. Having an objective at all times kept me hooked on the game. Or at least, objectives are perfect for stringing you along until the factory sim element gets its claws in you. Once the big machine gets going, you don’t need anything else to maintain momentum.

The complete list of additions in Palworld 1.0 is downright intimidating. You can read the whole thing on their Steam page, but the highlights are remarkable. 72 new Pals, the Sunreach region, the World Tree, and an increased level cap all speak to a much larger, more complete game. There’s more of course, but the point remains – Palworld has undergone significant changes since the early access days.

This new version of Palworld still has some flaws, to be fair. The laptop I’m using is decently powerful, but I encountered a handful of framerate dips regardless. More important than the tiny performance issues is the core gameplay loop. Things hum along at a more relatable pace than ever before, sure. But you’re still faced with a pretty murderous grind. Pal levels creep upward slowly, and getting through that tech trees gets daunting quite quickly. While things start out breezy enough, the endgame is strictly for simulation psychopaths.

By which I mean the truly dedicated. Which is totally fine! There’s a fascinating disconnect between the monster battling and the base building. You can immerse yourself in one and ignore the other, at least for a hefty chunk of playtime. Although perhaps my impressions of the battling are skewed by hands off it all is. Your Pals run on autopilot, both in battle and beyond it. So for me, the fights are a diversion from my tiny empire.

In that regard, Palworld remains a specialized interest. Either you’re ready to get lost in the details of empire expansion and monster murder, or you’ll quickly lose momentum. The quest system, new content, and expanded Pal roster are all incidental in the face of this essential truth. The gooey caramel center that is the gameplay loop is more or less the same as it ever was. My mind was changed about this game, true. But I’m prone to hyper focus and bouts of mania. So a vast and ruthless machine like Palworld is straight up catnip for my badly wired brain.

The 1.0 release of Palworld presents a very different game than the original early access version. The quest system has been revamped, the map has been expanded, and civilization is scattered everywhere. But the gameplay loop is still pretty relentless. Plus, the rough edges haven’t been completely removed. If the old game was almost it for you, this new iteration might be exactly what you yearned for. But Palworld 1.0 is still an acquired taste.

***A Steam key was provided by the publisher***
